PSA: Check Your Happy Dragon Orders – Hidden Charges and Mispriced Items

I’ve been a loyal customer of Happy Dragon for several years now, frequently placing orders over $30+. Recently, I decided to question an overcharge I noticed—because this has been happening to me every time I’ve placed an order by phone. My total from the Happy Dragon Restaurant pamphlet came out to be $34.25, but I was charged $35.25. When I asked about the extra $1, I was told by the rude lady it was a “delivery fee.”

I’ve been using their most recent July 2025 menu pamphlet, which replaced the older version a few months ago. Nowhere on this updated menu is a $1 delivery fee mentioned—only a $15 minimum for delivery is clearly listed. After looking further into the charges, I discovered that they automatically include a can of soda with every order—even when I didn’t ask for one—and quietly add a $1 charge for it.

The pamphlet also makes no mention of a free soda with a minimum order, further confirming that the soda is not complimentary but is instead being charged to the customer without consent.

When my food was delivered, I asked the friendly delivery driver if there was a $1 delivery charge or soda fee. He seemed confused, said he wasn’t aware of such a charge, and advised me to ask the restaurant directly. That raised further concerns—even the delivery staff aren’t aware of what customers are being billed for.

There was also a separate instances where I ordered only Chicken with Broccoli and white rice which is priced at $11.50 under the “Chicken” section of the menu pamphlet or only Beef with Broccoli and white rice which is priced at $11.75 under the “Beef” section of the menu pamphlet. Instead, I was charged for both orders under the “Combination Platters” section priced at $13.50 each, which includes pork fried rice and an egg roll—neither of which were included in my order upon delivery. This caused me to be overcharged for an incomplete combo meal I never ordered to begin with, and it’s happened more than once.

While these may seem like small charges, they’re being added without my knowledge or approval—and this has happened every time I’ve placed a phone order over several months, which suggests a clear, intentional pattern. Formal complaints have been filed with the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) & NYC 311. I hope Happy Dragon Chinese Restaurant takes responsibility and improves transparency in their pricing practices.

This is a PSA for all current and new customers placing phone orders: Always double-check your total and request a breakdown of charges, ensuring it matches what’s on their menu pamphlet (which is included on every delivery order). These unlisted fees and misclassifications are misleading and unfair to all Happy Dragon Chinese Restaurant customers.

I am truly very happy with my experience at Tino’s Delicatessen. Beyond offering such high-quality products, I really appreciate and value Rosa’s effort, care, and attention.

Thank you, Rosa. I will definitely continue ordering from Tino’s.

Tino's Delicatessen, Arthur Avenue, The Bronx, NY is in New York City gem!

There’s so much history with this unique, large oval shaped delicatessen, a mini Italian, grocery store, a few tables to dine in plus old photos and Italian-American memorabilia!
I felt so grateful and honored to meet & chat with the owners, Jon Carlo and and his wife Rosa. Jon Carlo explained how we purchased it directly from Tito I think about 28 years ago!

Although they seem to cater more to take out, I was so grateful Rosa was able to accommodate my request for their homemade lentil soup to be heated up in one of their bowls! (Otherwise typically served in Styrofoam bowls).

Unfortunately, the meal went downhill after the first bite. The ribs were mostly bone, and when I finally got to the meat, the outer layer was severely overcooked—so tough it felt like chewing on wet cardboard. The meat underneath wasn’t much better, with a rubbery texture that made it difficult to eat. By the end of the meal, my jaw was honestly tired from all the chewing.

The one standout was the BBQ sauce. It was excellent—flavorful without being overpowering. The yellow rice was also cooked perfectly: moist, firm, and paired really well with the sauce.

Sadly, the ribs were a major disappointment and felt badly overcooked. In the end, it felt like I paid $16.88 for a plate of BBQ sauce and rice.

review_text:
An incredible Jesuit University in the Bronx.

First I'd like to address the negative reviews. It is a secure campus so no you can't take a walk on the closed secure campus just because you feel like it. Imagine the arrogance of people to leave a negative review of an incredible historic university just because they were told NO.
Then there are the handful of haters who didn't get their fannys patted whole they were students or others who got rejected.. boo hoo.

Now onto the review. Fordham is an incredible university with a global reach.
My wife is an alum and we are on campus all the time and are very involved with the school.
First the physical campus is amazing. Rose Hill is sprawling and beautiful with a ton of green space and mature trees and plantings.
The buildings are beautiful and the new student center is an amazing space.
The sports facilities are great and if you have the chance you should try to get down there for a game whether it's football, basketball , water polo or even rugby. No matter what sport you go to see, it's always a great time.
The staff and the students are always friendly and welcoming !
After you graduate, the connection doesn't end there. The alumni association is strong and holds events all over the country.
We were in Florida and the Fordham baseball team was playing Florida Atlantic University and Fordham had an alumni tailgate at FAU before the game !
Homecoming weekend is a great time to be on campus. The tent on Edwards Parade is a great time as is the tailgate lot which is packed with Fordham pride.
Homecoming always starts with the Ram Run which I proudly run each year.
Academically, Fordham is stronger than ever ! Besides Rose Hill there is the Lincoln Center campus, the London Campus, the Westchester campus and even a biological field station in Westchester.
Fordham also nurtures a students spiritual needs. The campus ministry is strong and well rounded. The campus church is beautiful and we attend Christmas Eve Mass there each year.
Yes the tuition is expensive but you get what you pay for.  The university just received a  $100 million donation to build a new STEM building and increase the schools offerings I'm the sciences.
The school offers a wide array of undergrad and post grad degrees and the networking of the alums allows for greater job opportunities upon graduation.
Look, no school is perfect but Fordham is a fine example of Jesuit higher education and deserves a look from anyone considering higher education.

456 New Shanghai on Mott Street is a traditional Chinatown restaurant with a menu built around Shanghainese cooking and familiar Chinese comfort food. The restaurant is particularly associated with soup dumplings, making it an interesting option for people exploring different dumpling restaurants in the neighbourhood.

Xiao long bao are the main attraction. The dumplings contain meat filling and broth inside a delicate wrapper, requiring careful preparation to maintain the structure during steaming. The wrapper should be thin enough to avoid overwhelming the filling but strong enough to contain the soup.

The combination of ginger and vinegar traditionally served with soup dumplings adds acidity and freshness, balancing the richness of the meat.

The restaurant also offers noodle dishes, vegetables and more substantial preparations suitable for sharing. A combination of dumplings, stir-fried greens and noodles creates a more varied meal than ordering several similar appetizers.

The dining room is straightforward and practical, with bright lighting and a busy atmosphere. Tables turn over relatively quickly, particularly during lunch, and the restaurant is better suited to an informal meal than an extended fine-dining experience.

One advantage is the broad menu, which makes it possible for groups to choose between familiar Chinese dishes and more specialized Shanghainese preparations.

The location on Mott Street is convenient for exploring Chinatown, with Little Italy only a short walk away.

456 New Shanghai is especially interesting for people who enjoy traditional Chinese dumplings and want a restaurant focused on familiar regional cooking rather than elaborate presentation.

A few friends and I tried this beautiful new Greek restaurant in SoHo this week, and it was an amazing experience from start to finish! The restaurant itself is absolutely stunning, with a gorgeous atmosphere and such a great vibe. The food was incredibly delicious, and the service was truly top-notch. Every detail was thoughtfully done, making it the perfect spot for a night out with friends. Highly recommend! We will definitely be back!

If you’re looking for a fresh and exciting interpretation of Greek cuisine, look no further. This is THE place to experience it in NYC.

From beginning to end, our experience was nothing short of exceptional. Chef Nicholas Poulmentis and his talented team have created something truly special, seamlessly blending the soul of traditional Greek cuisine with modern creativity, refined techniques, and an extraordinary attention to detail.

Every dish we experienced was thoughtfully composed, beautifully presented, and executed with remarkable precision. We began with an impressive selection of starters, including the black truffle tarama, tuna tartare, beet salad, garides loukoumades, xtapodi, and kalamarakia. Each dish delivered its own distinct combination of flavors and textures, showcasing both the quality of the ingredients and the creativity behind the menu.

For our main courses, we shared the xtenia, branzino, Dover sole, and crab gogigies. The xtenia, in particular, was so extraordinary that we ordered it three times throughout the evening. That alone should tell you everything you need to know!

Dessert was equally memorable. We explored several offerings, including the ice cream, made fresh daily, and a selection of traditional Greek sweets reimagined with elegance and a thoughtful contemporary presentation. It was a beautiful conclusion to an already remarkable culinary journey.

Equally deserving of recognition is the beautifully curated wine list, which complements the cuisine exceptionally well, alongside an inventive cocktail menu that captures the essence of Greece and transports you straight to the Mediterranean.

Beyond the food and drinks, the hospitality was outstanding. The entire team was warm, knowledgeable, attentive, and genuinely accommodating, handling our numerous requests with professionalism and grace. It is clear that the same level of care and attention invested in the cuisine extends to every aspect of the guest experience.

As someone who deeply appreciates Greek cuisine, I can confidently say that this is far more than another Greek restaurant. It is a serious gastronomic destination that celebrates its heritage while confidently pushing culinary boundaries.

If you love Greek food, appreciate exceptional hospitality, and are looking for a truly memorable dining experience, I cannot recommend this restaurant highly enough.

My advice? Make your reservation now, before this hidden gem becomes the NYC dining phenomenon it is undoubtedly destined to be.

Paesano of Mulberry Street has been part of Little Italy since 1961, and its menu reflects the traditional Italian-American cooking that made this neighbourhood famous. Rather than focusing on elaborate plating or unusual ingredients, the restaurant concentrates on familiar pasta dishes, chicken, veal and seafood.

Chicken Parmesan is one of the most representative choices. The combination of breaded chicken, tomato sauce and melted cheese is straightforward, but the preparation depends on maintaining the texture of the chicken without allowing the sauce to make the coating excessively soft.

The pasta dishes offer a range of traditional sauces, from tomato-based preparations to richer cream and meat combinations. The restaurant is also known for its Trio Pasta, which allows diners to explore several pasta preparations in one meal instead of committing to a single sauce.

The dining room has a warm, old-fashioned atmosphere, with a more intimate feeling than some of the larger restaurants along Mulberry Street. It's the sort of setting that suits a family meal, especially when different people want different Italian-American favourites.

The restaurant's position in the middle of Little Italy makes it convenient for walking around the neighbourhood before or after dinner. At the same time, Mulberry Street is heavily visited, and the surrounding area can become noisy and crowded.

Paesano is best understood as a traditional neighbourhood restaurant rather than an experimental Italian kitchen. Its appeal is the continuity of familiar dishes and the atmosphere of an establishment that has remained associated with Little Italy for generations.

We began with the Primi Piccolo: smoked salmon with lemon chive crema. It was delicate yet full of flavor, with more than enough for two people. Next, I ordered the Calabrian Fusilli, while my wife chose the Butternut Squash Agnolotti. She raved about the squash with amaretti. Although I did not try her dish, the smile on her face told the story. My fusilli had just the right amount of spice. I know it sounds like a cliché, but even fantastic feels like an understatement. For our main courses, I ordered The San Domenico, a roasted pork chop, and my wife chose Modena, the slow-roasted duck breast. This time we shared, and we were very satisfied with both selections—the flavor profiles were oh so good! We still smile when we talk about the experience. I tip my hat to Michael and his team. The people, the atmosphere, and, of course, the food make Scalini Fedeli a must-try. Thank you for kicking off our 38th anniversary evening with great food and wonderful memories. Next time we’re in town, we will be back.

Having finally made its highly anticipated Manhattan debut after years of speculation following the shuttering of Chef Cesar Ramirez’s Brooklyn counter, it can safely be said that César is one of New York’s most scrutinized tickets, eye-popping prices nonetheless commanding frequent sell-outs for the few seats available.

Operating with a strict booking policy, a seat secured via the online portal months prior offers an experience that is technique-driven to the highest degree, rewarding those lucky enough to attend with pristine ingredients and flawless classical execution, though astronomical up-sells for “supplements” seem both unnecessary and out of place in 2* environs.

Staffed by a personable front-of-house team working in perfect harmony with a whisper-quiet kitchen, the sleek, minimalist room leaves much to be desired in terms of warmth, making one wonder for how long hyper-refined precision is “enough” to justify the escalating cost and the Mexico City native’s lightning rod for controversy.

Beginning with an array of finger-foods, two-spoons of Tomato Sorbet cleanses the palate before things accelerate rapidly, a delicate web of Kisu weaved into a shatteringly crisp potato casing trading honors with sweet Royal Red Shrimp tucked inside a Monaka shell and snappy Aji balancing a brittle Nori Chip.

Executed with intense focus, the margin for error limited as a result, Crab wrapped in Feuillette de Bric shows a robust crack while signature Sea Urchin layered with Black Truffle atop buttery Brioche achieves an immediate melange of temperatures and rich textures.

Moving into the plated courses, raw Hamachi stands tall alongside pickled Fennel and a vibrant Cucumber Herb dressing, though it is a perfectly pearlescent tranche of Madai resting in silky Chardonnay wine sauce that truly bridges French technique with Japanese ingredients.

Heavy hitters conclude via spoon-tender milk-fed Veal sourced from Southwest France, the accompanying Red Pearl Onion Purée deeply savory, though subsequent transitions into a light palate cleanser of Cherry and Yogurt with Riesling Gelée are well-paced before a frozen Dulce de Leche Soufflé and classic Petite Fours send guests into the night.

In the city that defines fine dining in the Western Hemisphere, this restaurant stands out. Every dish was perfectly executed, and the beautiful presentation enhanced, rather than distracted from, the flavors of the main ingredients. Each dish was cooked and seasoned just right. We didn't do the wine pairing, but the sommelier was very accommodating and offered exceptional wines by the glass. The staff was friendly and interesting. The chef was present and involved in every aspect of the dinner; he was personable, opinionated, and engaging. We rarely return to the same restaurant, but we may have to make this a tradition on our annual New York visit. For us, it certainly surpassed two three-Michelin-star restaurants we ate at during the same weekend in the city.

Chef César Ramirez delivers a remarkable combination of culinary creativity, exceptional ingredients, and flawless execution.

The scallop with caviar was delicious and perfectly balanced. The Wagyu beef was outstanding, as was the sea bass. The lamb was another highlight, incredibly tender and perfectly cooked.

The selection of amuse-bouches and desserts was equally impressive, creative, delicious, and memorable.

Service was excellent, attentive and polished, and welcoming throughout the evening.

A truly memorable evening and easily one of the finest dining experiences in New York.

I hesitated to write this review until I learned the final cost of our evening. After all, I had chosen HUSO for a special occasion and approached the experience with genuine excitement and high expectations. My guests and I appreciate  fine dining and know it is about far more than the food alone. It is the thoughtfulness of the service, the intention of each course, and the feeling that every detail has been considered. Unfortunately, HUSO fell short in several important respects.

For three guests, our bill came to approximately $4,000 for a bottle of champagne, the chef’s tasting menu, and the “Send” experience. At that price point, we expected an exceptional, memorable evening. Instead, we left feeling underwhelmed and questioning the value of the experience.

We arrived early for our reservation but were directed to a nearby bar while waiting for our table. We understood that the restaurant had limited space, and we appreciated being offered a complimentary glass of champagne when we were eventually seated approximately 20 minutes late. It was a gracious gesture, although the delay itself was disappointing.

The greater issue was a lack of clarity surrounding the “Send” option. We were presented with a card outlining the menu options, wine pairing, and additions of truffle and caviar, but we were never given a clear understanding of what the experience would actually entail. A menu or a more detailed explanation of the courses and supplements would have helped us make an informed decision. For an experience at this price point, transparency should be part of the hospitality.

The service was inconsistent and, at times, lacked the precision one expects from a restaurant positioning itself at this level. With three guests at the table, dishes were frequently delivered by two servers, occasionally resulting in garnishes falling during presentation. Sauces spilled onto the tablecloth, and the delivery of tea lacked even the basic coordination needed to identify which guest had ordered which variety. Multiple dessert courses also felt excessive rather than thoughtfully paced. These may seem like small details individually, but in fine dining, details are the experience.

Most disappointing was the caviar service. We had specifically expressed our excitement about it, yet a dedicated caviar presentation was never offered. Given HUSO’s association with a caviar boutique, this felt like a particularly missed opportunity. Instead, caviar appeared repeatedly as a garnish, often accompanied by generous amounts of truffle.

Caviar and truffle are both luxurious ingredients, but using them liberally does not necessarily elevate a dish. In our experience, the truffle frequently overwhelmed the delicate, briny character of the caviar. We would have much preferred a thoughtful, standalone bite—a blini or potato with a carefully considered portion of caviar—that allowed the ingredient to speak for itself. Had we understood that this would be the predominant approach, we would have reconsidered the “Send” option altogether.

There is no denying that the food was artistic and beautifully presented. However, visual presentation can only take a dish so far. We found the flavors themselves surprisingly pedestrian for a meal of this ambition and cost. Luxury ingredients, elaborate plating, and theatrical presentation should complement exceptional cooking, not substitute for it.

We did not expect a restaurant to reinvent gastronomy, nor did we expect perfection. We simply expected the quality of the food, the execution of the service, and the overall experience to justify the extraordinary price. At approximately $4,000 for three people, the evening should have been genuinely memorable for all the right reasons.

Unfortunately, HUSO did not deliver that experience for us. The potential is evident, but the execution, flavor, and value did not align with the restaurant’s positioning. For a special occasion at this price point, we expected to leave impressed. Instead, we left disappointed.

Easy to find on Bowey st. In Manhattan's Chinatown (1/2 block south of the iconic Canal st). Looks a little plain on the outside. My friend Jenny (a Manhattan Chinatown born and raised native) ordered seafood on crispy noodles. She shared  some with 3 of us and still had alot for herself. I tasted one of the shrimps. It was a big tasty shrimp, marinated in congee sauce. I was surprised there was so much, in an individual serving plate. Another person ordered a wonton noodle dish, which looked like a 2 - 3 pound bowl. I  bet she couldn't finish it (although she did). MY MEAL; I ordered the roasted duck (seoi siu aap - in Cantonese) on white rice. Like the others, my meal came out in about 10 minutes and was a huge dish. There were 10 large pieces of duck layed, on a fluffy bed of white rice, with a sided of steamed vegetables. The duck was a bit plain. Although, when I added "THEIR" soy sauce on it, the flavour was better. I said "THEIR" soy sauce because, it was sweeter than most soy sauces and it was a "tad" bit thicker. This is a soy sauce you'll want to take home. Actually, the fact that the duck came without sauce is a good thing. I've had  duck in the past and the sauce did not always agree to my liking. The meat was tender and succulent. On the whole, it was better than"marginally good" Be clear, I definitely enjoyed it down to the last bite. It just didn't stand out from the other roasted duck dishes out there. A strange (still ok) thing; there weren't any fortune cookies? 🤔They did however, have "Chinese doughnuts" - for $2.50. It's an oversized wobbly shaped doughnut, 3X the size of a normal doughnut with confectionery sugar. This was a first for me, it being more a novelty. The big shock, was the bill. With separate checks, I had roasted duck on white rice and a Chinese beer. With tax, the bill came out to $14.50! With what I got, I  thought this was going to be a $20 bill,( just for the food alone). My friend Jenny said, at the end of the meal, this restaurant is her favorite. She explained, she always has enough leftovers, to take home and the price is great. This restaurant is a few blocks away from the court houses in lower Manhattan and can get predictably crowded, during the lunch hour. We went on a Sunday, with mostly families at the other tables. We got a table immediately. The kitchen was small and well kept. It was nice to see my meals were coming from a properly kept kitchen. Please please don't be insulted by their manners, as sometimes they come off abrupt and short (even if you are Chinese). It's a Chinese/Chinatown restaurant "thing". Throughout time, I've become used to it and I don't even notice there manners anymore. Come tip time, I still give a generous tip anyway (they're still hard working people, with small wages).

Nyonya on Grand Street offers a completely different culinary tradition from the Italian and Cantonese restaurants surrounding it. The menu focuses on Malaysian cooking, which incorporates Malay, Chinese and Indian influences into dishes with distinctive combinations of spices, coconut milk and aromatic ingredients.

Roti canai is one of the most recognizable starters. The flatbread has a layered, slightly flaky texture and is served with curry sauce for dipping. The contrast between the bread and the richly seasoned sauce makes it a useful introduction to Malaysian food.

Curry laksa is another important preparation, combining noodles with a coconut-based curry broth. The dish can include seafood, tofu and other ingredients, creating a combination of creamy richness, spice and different textures.

Hainanese chicken rice offers a more restrained alternative. The chicken is accompanied by seasoned rice and sauces that provide additional flavour without overwhelming the meat.

The menu is extensive, which makes the restaurant particularly suitable for groups willing to share several dishes. Combining a curry, a noodle dish, vegetables and rice allows diners to explore different sides of Malaysian cooking.

The dining room is practical rather than elaborate, and the atmosphere is generally busy. Tables near the entrance may be less comfortable during cold weather because of the frequent movement of customers.

Nyonya is especially appealing for people who want something beyond the most familiar Chinese and Italian dishes in the neighbourhood. The combination of coconut, curry, noodles and traditional Malaysian preparations gives the restaurant a distinctive identity.

This is exactly what you want from a sit down Chinese restaurant. Delicious, American Chinese food (unless you can read the Chinese menu and unlock the interesting stuff) done very, very well.

We had the beef chow fun and the lychee pineapple duck.

The chow fun was dang near perfect. The only note I have is that it was a drop salty. Otherwise, perfect. The wok hei (that hard to quantify smoky flavor when you get really good Chinese food) is always what brings this dish together, and it was really kicking in this disk. The beef was tender but not falling apart, a good bite but not chewy. The bean sprouts were crisp and satisfying.

The duck was really a work of art. It's a very fatty dish, but the fat under the skin was perfectly rendered, and it melted in my mouth. The sauce was sweet without being sickly, and mixed very well with the white rice that came in the side. The skin on the duck was excellent. It's tossed in a sauce so it's not crispy, but it was so savory and flavorful.

Serafina TriBeCa is conveniently located right at West Broadway & Chambers, making it an easy, accessible stop steps from the red and blue train lines.

​I popped in for a quick bite and a cocktail, and both hit the mark. The Fig Old Fashioned was a standout—smooth, well-balanced, and a great twist on a classic. You immediately notice the intentionality behind the menu: alongside all the classic Italian favorites, the clearly labeled vegetarian and plant-forward selections make navigating dietary preferences effortless. The Spaghetti Squash was fresh, flavorful, and perfectly seasoned without feeling heavy.

​The vibe is lively yet comfortable; the moderate noise level makes it an ideal spot where you can actually hold a conversation. Logistically, the restrooms are located upstairs, where you’ll also find a separate seating area that looks perfect for hosting a private event or intimate gathering. They also have a rooftop space that I’ll definitely be checking out on my next visit.

​Quick, welcoming service and reliable quality—an easy downtown spot to bookmark.

review_text:
A truly beautiful, next-level hotel!

We stayed here for our honeymoon in January 2024. Before booking, we tried calling the hotel directly to see if they could offer a better rate than what was available online, but unfortunately, no luck, even though it was considered off-season.

For a hotel of this caliber, we expected a more personalized and attentive level of service. Concierge services were never offered or introduced to us, and the only honeymoon gesture we received was a few pieces of chocolate.

That said, we absolutely loved the location, interiors, bedding, and especially the beautiful marble! 😍

Definitely recommend the hotel for its stunning design and overall quality. However, I would have expected the staff to go the extra mile, especially for a honeymoon. The service felt a little dry and lacked the warmth and attention you would expect from a hotel of this level.

Double Crispy is one of my fave Chinatown bakeries; I’ve been coming here since 2018. Whenever I am in Chinatown, I try to stop by and pick up a couple things. Their variety of baos, baked goods, cakes, and egg tarts is incredible! Every year they put so much love and care into their moon cakes for mid autumn moon festival, and around lunar new year, they have endless traditional, lunar new year treats, and sweets for you to purchase. The staff is friendly and efficient. My personal faves are their moon cakes, Portuguese style egg tarts, sesame cookies (the thin flat ones at the front), the cha siu bao, pork floss bao, and the pineapple bao with egg custard inside! Their HK style sponge cake is
also a hit; my 4-yo is obsessed with it! You can also get their packs or chicken/cabbage bao for an amazing value, which I occasionally get. They keep well in the freezer, and when you want, you can pop some
Out, steam them, and they are super fresh and fluffy! Love this family owned business. Their story (as featured by NYT food on YouTube) is just so touching and heart warming. How can you not want to support them?!

I'm glad I went with that suggestion because the coffee was stellar, and was just what I needed. It had a very well rounded, I'd say full flavor to it that was satisfying with every sip, which I'm sure speaks as much to the bean as it does to the person pouring it.

My wife had a latte with toasted oat syrup and while I can't speak in depth for her I can say she enjoyed it.

After we finished our coffees the barista came around with some complimentary "dessert" drinks, which were a fantastic surprise as well. It really made us feel cared for and that on top of the very pleasant countenance of the individual feels above and beyond what I expect when getting coffee in the morning.

Was looking for a good coffee shop in the area and came across La Colombe Coffee Roasters. I had tried La Colombe before, so I brought my friends here to check it out as well.
Service was super quick, and everyone was really nice, from the server to our barista. I decided to try one of their seasonal drinks, the Iced Pumpkin Spice Draft Latte with oat milk. Their Draft Latte is a creamy, smooth cold coffee drink, and the pumpkin spice gives it that warm seasonal flavour without completely overpowering the coffee. The oat milk also made it extra smooth and creamy. Definitely a nice fall drink.
My friends tried a few different drinks as well:
Matcha Vanilla — The matcha was actually really good, with a nice balance between the earthy matcha and sweetness from the vanilla. Neither flavour overpowered the other.
Caramel Apple Latte — A nice combination of coffee, caramel and apple flavours. It had a good balance of sweetness and coffee, with the apple adding a subtle fruity touch rather than making it taste overly sweet.
Iced Vanilla Latte — Pretty much true to its name! A straightforward iced latte with a clear vanilla flavour. Simple, refreshing, and exactly what you'd expect.
The café itself was clean and has a smaller, cozy setup with around 7 stools for seating, along with a bench running along the entire back wall. It seems like a good spot to grab a quick coffee or sit for a little while.
Overall, a quick and pleasant visit with friendly service and a good selection of drinks. The seasonal Pumpkin Spice Draft Latte was definitely a fun one to try.

An excellent Italian restaurant in Little Italy in New York, this is a small, family-run restaurant that makes excellent dishes with great service. Everything we ate was delicious. Each pasta dish (homemade) costs between $25-30.

Benito One is one of the smaller, older-style Italian restaurants along Mulberry Street, and its compact dining room gives it a different personality from the larger establishments nearby. The restaurant has been associated with Little Italy since the late 1960s, maintaining the traditional trattoria approach rather than adopting a contemporary restaurant design.

Chicken Parmigiana is one of the recognizable dishes. The preparation brings together breaded chicken, tomato sauce and melted mozzarella, with the quality depending on the balance between the crisp coating and the richness of the sauce. Too much sauce can overwhelm the chicken, so the proportions are particularly important.

The pasta selection includes familiar Italian-American preparations, including richer sauces and traditional tomato-based dishes. The menu is aimed at people who enjoy recognizable comfort food rather than elaborate tasting menus.

Large windows allow diners to watch the activity outside on Mulberry Street. The combination of traditional décor, background music and close seating creates a more intimate atmosphere, although the small dining room can become noisy when several tables are occupied.

The restaurant is well positioned for a meal while exploring Little Italy, Chinatown and nearby Nolita. It also offers the kind of familiar menu that works for families with different preferences.

Benito One's appeal is its old-fashioned neighbourhood character. It isn't trying to compete with modern restaurants through architectural spectacle or experimental ingredients. The focus remains on traditional Italian-American dishes and the atmosphere of a small restaurant in one of Manhattan's most recognizable historic neighbourhoods.

Xi'an Famous Foods on Bayard Street offers a very different style of Chinese cooking from the Cantonese restaurants that dominate much of Chinatown. The menu draws inspiration from the cuisine of Xi'an in northwestern China, where wheat-based noodles, cumin, chili and bold seasonings play an important role.

The spicy cumin lamb noodles are one of the signature dishes. The noodles are wide, irregular and deliberately chewy, providing a substantial texture that works well with the strongly seasoned lamb. Cumin adds a warm, earthy flavour, while chili oil contributes heat and richness.

Another distinctive preparation is the hand-ripped noodle dish, where the irregular shape of the noodles allows the sauce to cling to different surfaces. This creates a completely different eating experience from thin Cantonese egg noodles or Italian pasta.

The restaurant also offers meat-filled flatbread sandwiches, where the contrast between the bread and the richly seasoned filling is central to the dish.

The dining room is simple and practical. Customers typically order at a counter or kiosk, collect their food and clear their own tables. It's designed for quick meals rather than extended dining.

Spice levels are an important consideration. Some dishes are intensely seasoned, and people unfamiliar with northwestern Chinese cooking may find the combination of chili and cumin stronger than expected.

Xi'an Famous Foods is particularly interesting for anyone who wants to explore Chinese regional cooking beyond fried rice, dumplings and conventional noodle soup. The focus is firmly on the food rather than the surrounding décor.

Little Italy is one of those New York neighborhoods where, every once in a while, you find a place that feels like a passage to the past, and Caffe Roma is exactly that.

Founded in 1891, this cafe has managed to preserve something that is increasingly difficult to find in New York: the feeling of another era. In the middle of all the noise, movement, and constant change of the city, stepping inside feels like entering a little time capsule. And yes, the coffee is excellent, but Caffe Roma is about more than just coffee.

Take a moment to look around. The details on the walls, the ceiling, the old-fashioned décor... they are all part of the experience. This place has been collecting stories for more than a century, and you can feel that history while sitting at your table, enjoying a coffee and an Italian dessert. With just a little imagination, you might even travel back in time for a few minutes.

My personal favorite is the affogato. I love the combination of hot espresso and cold, creamy vanilla gelato, and this is exactly the kind of place where it just feels right to order one.

But you really can´t go wrong here. Whether you are looking for a good coffee, something sweet, or a traditional Italian dessert, there are plenty of options to enjoy.

Whether you are visiting New York for the first time or you are a local who has walked throught Little Italy a hundred times, Caffe Roma is one of those places worth experiencing at least once.

I visited AIRE on Sunday to treat myself to a massage and a relaxing spa day after a long run. The massage was absolutely fantastic. My massage therapist was extremely professional, skilled, and clearly knew what she was doing. I thoroughly enjoyed the experience.

The bath area was beautiful, clean, peaceful, and very well maintained. The atmosphere was incredibly calming, and I enjoyed spending time in the different pools. However, the overall temperature was noticeably colder than I expected. Even the warmer pools weren’t particularly warm, and the facility itself felt quite chilly whenever I was out of the water.

Unfortunately, things got worse when I returned to the locker room. I was already feeling cold, and the locker room was even chillier. When I tried to shower, the water simply wouldn’t heat up. I had to switch between three different showers, and it took nearly ten minutes to find one with reasonably warm water. Other women were experiencing the same issue and commenting on how long it was taking for the water to heat up. By that point, I was wet, freezing, and literally shivering. Even when I finally managed to shower, the water was only lukewarm.

I ended up feeling unwell afterward and developed a cold, which was certainly not how I expected to feel after a relaxing spa day.

Overall, AIRE is a beautiful space with excellent massage services, and there is a lot to appreciate about the experience. However, for a luxury spa at this price point, maintaining comfortable temperatures throughout the facility and ensuring reliably hot showers should be a basic expectation. I really hope management addresses this, as it would make an otherwise lovely experience so much better.

AIRE Ancient Baths in Tribeca offers an enchanting escape from NYC’s bustle. The candlelit interiors, subdued lighting, and ancient-inspired music create a beautifully moody yet serene atmosphere.

The hot pool was soothing, though the jacuzzi felt more like a roaring rapid than a tranquil soak. The cold plunge was invigorating but disappointingly shallow. The steam room was comfortably hot, although a slightly higher temperature would have made the experience even more satisfying.

Our package included a 30-minute massage with firm yet relaxing pressure. While pleasant, it was ultimately unmemorable given the premium price. The true allure of AIRE lies in its bathing facilities.

Hospitality was excellent, cleanliness impeccable, and locker room amenities equally impressive.

Overall, a splendid spa experience with captivating ambiance and pristine facilities. I would gladly return for the baths but forgo the body treatments, as their value doesn’t quite justify the indulgence.

They have SO many options, and I genuinely enjoyed taking my time looking through everything. I especially loved finding their Asian-inspired charms and was able to create my own little jade collection, which made the experience feel even more personal and meaningful to me.

If you enjoy charm bars, personalized accessories, matcha, or simply discovering unique local businesses, Quirk Haus is definitely worth checking out. Such a fun activity to do with friends or even as a little solo creative date while exploring Brooklyn!

Eulalie was a magical dining experience. The greeting from Tina and her team was warm, attending to every detail throughout the meal, including discussing our my leftover dessert would be perfect in the morning as breakfast. The food was spectacular. Highly recommend the wine pairing which elevated every dish. I wish I had taken more pics, but I could wait to dig in as each hit the table. Everyone should have a beautiful meal at Eulalie!!!

Simply incredible experience. Were we treated so nicely because we were first timers?? Food was stellar.
Not enough to lower a star but rushed at first to order drinks, based on expectations from the online description. This became understandable. They do state that you can have the table for the evening, however, other diners were waiting for us to vacate our table.

From the moment we walked in the door at Eulalie, we knew we were in for a special evening.

From the lighting, to the colors, the decor, the jazz soundtrack at the perfect volume, and the generous table sizes and spacing; this is a meticulously designed and exceptionally comfortable room. It inspired me to take out my camera.

Even the acoustics were notable, either due to some kind of engineering wizardry, or because it’s just a room with good bones. At its busiest, it wasn’t noisy. And towards the end of the night, it wasn’t echoey or empty sounding.

The staff were fantastic. Everyone there truly seemed to enjoy what they were doing. Within a few minutes of sitting down, we were made to feel like regulars, even though this was our first visit.

Our main waiter Bennett, is a real renaissance man. Part waiter, part sommelier, part mâitre fromager. He and the rest of the team perfectly balanced professional and fun.

Little gifts appeared throughout the night… an extra wine pour here, some champagne there, amuses, an extra dessert.

The food was fantastic overall. The cheeses were sublime. The wine pairing we did was among the most inventive and thoughtful we’ve ever experienced.

The coconut cake was excellent but the pot de crème was a show stopper.

We spent a delightful 3+ hours at Eulalie, which in no way felt long. I told our waiter that the entire experience sort of felt like seeing a great off Broadway play and hanging out with the cast after the show. We laughed with chef Chip and his kitchen. We toasted with Tina. It was an extended whirlwind of culinary magic and tastefully choreographed joy.

On reflection, it also occurred to me that I got the same feels from dining at Eulalie as I did from watching Big Night. I can’t really think of a higher compliment for a restaurant.

The main course and appetizers are great, the dessert is so-so — it’s not bad, it’s just the rest has a sophisticated presentation and flavor but the desserts are more of the homemade, big portion pieces of cakes.

Service is unique, it is attentive but somewhat confusing (we were asked for dessert choices 3 times by 3 different people and waited 20min to get a menu since seated — feels particularly long when you are hungry!).

Overall an interesting idea and the slow pace does give some refreshing and peaceful undertones to a weekend evening in this busy city 🍎

The staff then tried to seat us near the loud crowd, and we requested another move. Eventually, we were given an appropriately sized table away from the noise.

Family-Style Appetizers

·         Chicken Satay: Just okay.

·         Glazed Prawns (2): Great.

·         Vegetarian Potstickers: Just okay and served without dipping sauce.

Family-Style Entrées

·         Ma Mignon: Great.

·         Green Prawns: Good.

·         Sea Bass: Bad and very bland.

Family-Style Sides

Overall Impression

Il Cortile is one of the restaurants that still represents the older character of Manhattan's Little Italy. Operating since 1975, it has a traditional Italian dining atmosphere that feels very different from the newer restaurants in Nolita. The most interesting feature is the glass-ceilinged garden dining room, which creates a sense of openness despite being surrounded by the buildings of Lower Manhattan.

The fettuccine di Parma is one of the dishes worth knowing about. It's a rich pasta preparation where the texture of the noodles and the consistency of the sauce are particularly important. Rather than relying on an enormous quantity of ingredients, the dish follows the traditional Italian approach of combining pasta with a carefully prepared sauce.

The restaurant's menu concentrates on Italian classics, including pasta, seafood and meat dishes. The setting makes it especially suitable for a longer family dinner rather than a quick meal between sightseeing stops.

One thing worth considering is where you sit. The garden room offers a noticeably different atmosphere from the front dining area. The restaurant also has several private dining spaces, so larger groups can be accommodated without necessarily occupying the main dining room.

Mulberry Street becomes extremely crowded during weekends and festivals, and the surrounding noise is part of the neighbourhood's character. Il Cortile is particularly interesting for people who want a traditional Italian-American dining experience in a restaurant with genuine neighbourhood history.

Xi'an Famous Foods on Bayard Street offers a very different style of Chinese cooking from the Cantonese restaurants that dominate much of Chinatown. The menu draws inspiration from the cuisine of Xi'an in northwestern China, where wheat-based noodles, cumin, chili and bold seasonings play an important role.

The spicy cumin lamb noodles are one of the signature dishes. The noodles are wide, irregular and deliberately chewy, providing a substantial texture that works well with the strongly seasoned lamb. Cumin adds a warm, earthy flavour, while chili oil contributes heat and richness.

Another distinctive preparation is the hand-ripped noodle dish, where the irregular shape of the noodles allows the sauce to cling to different surfaces. This creates a completely different eating experience from thin Cantonese egg noodles or Italian pasta.

The restaurant also offers meat-filled flatbread sandwiches, where the contrast between the bread and the richly seasoned filling is central to the dish.

The dining room is simple and practical. Customers typically order at a counter or kiosk, collect their food and clear their own tables. It's designed for quick meals rather than extended dining.

Spice levels are an important consideration. Some dishes are intensely seasoned, and people unfamiliar with northwestern Chinese cooking may find the combination of chili and cumin stronger than expected.

Xi'an Famous Foods is particularly interesting for anyone who wants to explore Chinese regional cooking beyond fried rice, dumplings and conventional noodle soup. The focus is firmly on the food rather than the surrounding décor.

On Saturday, I placed an order for two drinks with “Jay” (I think he said), the barista, and specifically requested no ice. Despite spending a couple of minutes clarifying exactly what I wanted, he made both drinks as slushies. When I pointed out that I had requested no ice, he told me that the mochi matcha was supposed to be a slushy. I explained that I understood that, but I wanted a cold matcha latte with milk and mochi paste, without ice.

I initially thanked him and left, but after taking a sip, I realized I couldn’t drink it that way. I returned and politely asked if he could remake the drinks. He refused.

I spend at least $80 a month here and always leave a tip because I genuinely enjoy supporting this business. I understand that mistakes happen, but what disappointed me most was the lack of willingness to find a solution to a simple, reasonable request.

I hope the owners see this review and take it as constructive feedback. I would love to continue coming here, but I also believe that listening to customers and providing good service when something goes wrong are essential to maintaining their loyalty.

an art cafe hidden in plain sight of Atelier Jolie, an arts collective / cultural center in NoHo, which was opened by Angelina Jolie. those in the arts scene might recognize the address as it was occupied by Andy Warhol and Jean-Michael Basquiat a long time ago...and it’s formerly the home of the speak-easy-ish restaurant Bohemian. Eat Offbeat operates the cafe area and is an NYC-based organization that employs refugees and immigrants to celebrate and elevate the craft & artisanship of cooking from around the world. the cafe space feels like an art gallery--adorned with art and art-centric books, somewhat intimate seating, and bright art lighting positioned above. the ambiance evokes upscale with the touch of minimalism in the bare white walls but is welcoming in its curated cafe menu of coffees, teas, juices, and small bites. it's clear that the decor and vibe are to evoke creativity and thought as you enjoy a coffee or a bite. very much place to share, but also to protect its ethos of spirit. been here several times — enjoyed a cortado and Americano to-go. both were made proficiently. currently, the cafe uses a South American (maybe El Salvadoran?) medium roast coffee that has a pleasant deep nuttiness and a mildly sweet undertones  as a coffee. very much a smooth caffeine for the winter times. the last time i stopped here, ordered a Turkish coffee and enjoyed it at the cafe. not sure the “Turkish coffee” is actually traditional coffee from Turkey, but the coffee served in a Turkish style. it's served on a small silver tray where a "cezve" (the handled counter where the coffee is boiled),  fincan (the small 2 oz. cup) for slowly sipping the coffee, and a Syrian Barazak Cookie (there are two choices of sweets). it's very much an aesthetically pleasing presentation. the coffee is served hot as it foams up...the coffee tastes richer and thicker because it is served this way. it's fancy in a nonchalant way. Turkish coffee is meant to be enjoyed in a social way, so bring a friend! the service at Eat OffBeat is pleasant and hospitable. the barista is conscientious in the coffee-making and service. the patrons of the Atelier and the cafe  from my experience are from the arts world, but aren't pretentious or snooty which is refreshing. it is a nice respite from the hustle and bustle of the city and the hustle and bustle of tooo many coffee shops. take a breath here and enjoy art aka life.

We decided to try Bistrot Ha after seeing it on the NYT restaurant list, so expectations were fairly high. It's a tiny, intimate space with a very fish-sauce-forward menu.

The pear pie à la mode did redeem the evening somewhat—it was buttery, flaky pastry heaven and easily one of my favorite things we ate.

Amazing Market on the lower east side of Manhattan with such a deep rooted History. Goes all the way back to 1818 as a market house. Today, it offers many stores and restaurants inside. You can get everything from a Butcher, Fish Market, Spices, Pizza, Bakery, Cheese shop, a Bar and multiple restaurants and grocery stores. The 2nd floor has seating areas and restrooms. It's definitely worth the visit and checking what it has to offer for yourself. Even if it's just to grab a slice of Pizza and use the restroom after walking over the Williamsburg bridge like I do.
The New Museum is where I go when I want my assumptions about art challenged. The programming here is bold and genuinely interesting — never the safe choice, always worth the trip.

You start on the 4th floor and go down from there. The 4th and 3rd floors are very dark with disturbing images and sounds. Then as you get lower, there’s some Keith Haring and other works that are ok.

Ben was an amazing employee and so sweet. However, this museum did not do Arthur Jafra’s work justice. The lighting for the exhibit was not good. You couldn’t read the captions in most of the rooms. There was a lot of glare on the photos. Considering Jafra’s work is mostly photo and video, this took away from the experience.

Also, the new museum claims to care about social justice issues and yet literally deploys a private equity backed tech company for coat check when there’s literally no purpose of collecting people’s photos or phone numbers. Super creepy.

You can also add more toppings to the broth, extra charge.

Pro tip: This restaurant is cash only, so make sure to bring cash!

8282 was such a great experience from start to finish. The food was delicious, the service was excellent, and the overall vibe made it a perfect spot for a fun night out. I’d definitely recommend making reservations ahead of time, as this is a place worth planning for.

I loved how you could assemble your own little hand rolls, combining all the different textures and flavors in each bite. It was interactive, creative, and absolutely delicious.

PERILLA OIL PASTA — Angel hair pasta with soy sauce, perilla leaves, and seared branzino. Such an interesting combination of flavors, with the fragrant perilla bringing an Asian twist to the pasta. A great dish if you want something a little different from the usual.

8282 STEAK— Grilled hanger steak with mashed sweet potatoes and pine nut basil pesto. The steak had a delicious, savory flavor with an Asian-inspired profile that really stood out. Paired with the creamy sweet potato and fresh, nutty pesto, every component added something to the dish. A real burst of flavor!

Don't skip the drinks!

Shot of the Day — Let the bartenders surprise you with a mystery shot! It's a fun way to try something unexpected, challenge your palate, and keep everyone guessing what the flavor profiles are. Definitely adds to the experience.

White Rabbit Slush — A take on makgeolli, rum, and soju with a refreshing sweetness from lychee. Don't let the slushy texture fool you; this little drink packs a powerful punch! Fruity, floral, and dangerously easy to sip.

Between the inventive food, playful drinks, and attentive service, 8282 delivered a memorable night out. It's the kind of place where you want to order a few dishes to share, try something new, and enjoy the whole experience. Amazing food, amazing service, and a great time all around. an art cafe hidden in plain sight of Atelier Jolie, an arts collective / cultural center in NoHo, which was opened by Angelina Jolie. those in the arts scene might recognize the address as it was occupied by Andy Warhol and Jean-Michael Basquiat a long time ago...and it’s formerly the home of the speak-easy-ish restaurant Bohemian. Eat Offbeat operates the cafe area and is an NYC-based organization that employs refugees and immigrants to celebrate and elevate the craft & artisanship of cooking from around the world. the cafe space feels like an art gallery--adorned with art and art-centric books, somewhat intimate seating, and bright art lighting positioned above. the ambiance evokes upscale with the touch of minimalism in the bare white walls but is welcoming in its curated cafe menu of coffees, teas, juices, and small bites. it's clear that the decor and vibe are to evoke creativity and thought as you enjoy a coffee or a bite. very much place to share, but also to protect its ethos of spirit. been here several times — enjoyed a cortado and Americano to-go. both were made proficiently. currently, the cafe uses a South American (maybe El Salvadoran?) medium roast coffee that has a pleasant deep nuttiness and a mildly sweet undertones  as a coffee. very much a smooth caffeine for the winter times. the last time i stopped here, ordered a Turkish coffee and enjoyed it at the cafe. not sure the “Turkish coffee” is actually traditional coffee from Turkey, but the coffee served in a Turkish style. it's served on a small silver tray where a "cezve" (the handled counter where the coffee is boiled),  fincan (the small 2 oz. cup) for slowly sipping the coffee, and a Syrian Barazak Cookie (there are two choices of sweets). it's very much an aesthetically pleasing presentation. the coffee is served hot as it foams up...the coffee tastes richer and thicker because it is served this way. it's fancy in a nonchalant way. Turkish coffee is meant to be enjoyed in a social way, so bring a friend! the service at Eat OffBeat is pleasant and hospitable. the barista is conscientious in the coffee-making and service. the patrons of the Atelier and the cafe  from my experience are from the arts world, but aren't pretentious or snooty which is refreshing. it is a nice respite from the hustle and bustle of the city and the hustle and bustle of tooo many coffee shops. take a breath here and enjoy art aka life.

Caffè Dante – MacDougal Street, NYC

We visited Caffè Dante on a Saturday night. It’s a casual, lively spot with a vibrant bar scene, especially known for its cocktails. If you’re a cocktail lover, this is definitely a place to check out!

The food was excellent, from the appetizers to the main dishes and desserts. Everything we ordered was delicious and beautifully presented.

The atmosphere, however, was extremely loud inside especially on a Saturday night. Seating is quite tight, so don’t expect much personal space, although a cozy corner table might offer a little more privacy. They also have outdoor seating, which could be a nice alternative.

The crowd was mostly younger to middle-aged adults, with very few people in our age group (60s–70s). It definitely feels more like a trendy neighborhood hangout than a quiet dinner spot.

Overall, great food, a fun atmosphere, and a fantastic cocktail scene. We’d recommend it for anyone who enjoys a lively night out, but if you’re looking for a relaxed dinner with easy conversation, this might not be the best choice, especially on a Saturday night.

If your hours say you’re open at 12 PM, customers should reasonably be able to expect you to be open at 12 PM.

If that’s not possible, then please update your hours or communicate with your customers. I genuinely wanted to try this place, which is why I kept trying, but this experience has been incredibly irritating and disappointing.

the pizza is a-okay at Madison Street Pizza imo. obviously that is subjective but not every pizza slice you get in NYC  is going to be the greatest or worst. to me, it's very much in the middle--this would not be my go-to spot or a place to avoid. it's very much a neighborhood pizza place in the Two Bridges area on a quiet stretch of Madison Street. the walkdown pizzeria is in a small place below street level with a few seats squeezed into the space. the place is clean but has that worn-in coziness. the counter has a variety of pizza pies and slices on display. ordered a plain cheese slice to go. the ladies who worked there were very nice, quickly heated up my slice, and served up a hot out of the oven pizza slice on a paper plate. there's plenty of mozzarella cheese and sauce on the plain slice and had a fairly crispy bottom. however the slice really didn't come together for me--the flavor of the sauce was a bit too sweet and a bit tomato soup-y as there was too much of it on the slice in my opinion, the cheese was nice and melty, and the crust's bottom was crispy but the slice's crust was a bit thicker than a usual NYC slice and had a bit more readiness and chew to it. overall, the slice was fine as a quick bite. the style of the slice probably is more attuned to what the neighborhood wants than my preference in pizza. would i have a slice here if i were in the neighborhood? probably, but I wouldn't make a special trip for it. pizza preference is ultimately subjective and this place has its fans in this locale...so i ain't gunna hate. ha. also the prices here are not high for a single slice...they are reasonable. service was friendly. when it comes to pizza--to each, his or her own!

TSUKEMEN - You get a much thicker broth and a separate bowl of thick noodles. The thick noodles are more of an udon to me, but still perfectly bouncy. You take a portion of the noodles and dip into the broth, coating each noodle with that luxurious broth. This was good, but not as amazing as the Tontori. I had the chicken chashu and it was amazing. We had a wonderful experience at KALYE, a Filipino restaurant in New York that I highly recommend. We enjoyed traditional dishes served on banana leaves, which added a special touch to our meal. At KALYE, you have the option to eat with your hands or use clear plastic gloves—both ways are enjoyable!

The owner, Mr. Rob Mallari-D'Auria, was very engaging and made a point to visit each table to inquire about our experience and introduce himself. When he came to our table, we had the joy of sharing our Filipino heritage with him. My brother mentioned that we were born in the Philippines, which led to lots of laughter as we switched from English to Tagalog—except for my son, who was born here and hasn't learned Tagalog or our dialect, Pangalatok.

Mr. Rob was generous and offered us a complimentary shot, which was delightful, along with an amazing Ube Mocktail! I can't recommend the Ube sliders enough; they are a must-try for anyone planning to visit.

Overall, the food was fantastic, and the atmosphere was warm and welcoming. The staff, including Mr. Rob, were incredibly friendly and attentive. I will definitely be returning to KALYE for another wonderful meal!

Absolutely love Le Dive! We always have a wonderful time. Burak and Ike really go out of their way to build hospitality and curate an incredible environment for everyone. Would highly recommend!

Our lunch was so delicious, we returned that same evening for dinner!  Arman and Angelus were warm and gracious and made sure we had everything we wanted.  This is now our favourite restaurant in Manhattan!!

So strange, ordered many drinks and came with a big group- we were occasionally hitting our vapes the place was void of no smoking signs, usually you are allowed to vape in bars in NYC. Good was delicious and service was amazing. Started to get busy as we finished up and the amazing bartender was all of the place. Would definitely come back if I'm in the area again.

Overall we had a great experience. The food was fresh and flavorful, the service was attentive, and the staff was welcoming throughout the entire visit. Everything came out correctly and at a good pace. We really enjoyed the meal and would definitely recommend this place to others.
Best sports bar in downtown. Food, service, drinks all hit. Plus multiple TVs with games or fights are on. They also have a nice setup in front with a TV to sit outside.
Casa Colven is full of surprises. The food and drinks is so deliciously fresh and tasty 😋 You must come in for yourself to witness what Casa Colven bring to your table. Enjoy 😉
A small piece of Colombia and Venezuela, thank you for the wonderful ambiance and attention. It’s definitely worth it!

We stumbled across this incredible place and I couldn’t recommend it more; it’s so good that we went back a few times. The owner is an amazing woman and we had the best margaritas ever. It’s most definitely worth a visit!!! Can’t wait to come next time we’re back in town.

I do like this dunkin but I had to withhold one star because they do not carry jelly munchkins. If they bring them back, I will give this place 5 stars. The staff are friendly and they make my coffee well.

Waited far to long for my order. Then they gave me the wrong order. I pointed to the menu which I ordered from, thinking they couldn’t understand what I was asking for. They continued to make it wrong. I left without them offering a refund and I had no order.

After several bad experiences at this Dunkin I said maybe they improved and let me try again.  Welp I was wrong.   On Google it says the store closes at 7 pm.   I got there at 6:40 to redeem an offer for $2 coffee.   The ladies said they are closed so I left.  A few minutes later I passed by again, the front door is still open and see a man in there making a purchase.  I went in and said I thought you were close🤔.  One of the ladies said the man called ahead of time to get his order.   It was me and another customer they turned away.   I told the other customer “You know if they don’t want to serve us they don’t need our money”.   I will never set foot in this place again.  I’m all for supporting small business but they have to act like they want the support.

Horrible store. I came in and stood at the register for 24 minutes, not a hello, nobody took my order. This is so unprofessional they stared at me and continued to make drink after drink and never even said anything to me. They look so angry and miserable and do not care for the job. This was by far the worst Dunkin experience of my life. Pay attention to your staff because they are clearly unhappy.
This place makes good affordable food and has been serving the community for over 40 years. We need more places like this back in our communities.

The stars of the evening are the pieces of fish themselves. Even comparing our multiple sushi outings in Japan, Sugarfish's quality was bizarrely high - nearly every piece melted in our mouths. The no tipping policy - like Japan - is welcome. The sequential dishes brought out with their Trust Me kits are "omakase-like." The Minitable app phone wait system works well. A couple tiny critiques, which keeps Sugarfish from earning 5 stars overall. The rice is deliciously warm, but oversalted and not at all sticky; this makes it impossible to evert the sushi to dip the fish - and not the rice - in the soy sauce. There is no hashioki (tiny resting device) for your chopsticks, which must reside messily on your table between dishes. The small amount of wasabe provided to you tasted super hot without the front of the tongue subtlety of fresh horseradish; I strongly suspect it was "American wasabe-like" -  horseradish, mustard, green food coloring. Despite the slick wait system that uses the Minitable app and your cell phone, the young GenX's at check-in were relatively clueless and borderline incompetent.

Best place in all of Manhattan!  Lydia and Allison are the absolute best.  Just walk in, sit down and order the Trust Me. Allow the chefs to walk you through a omakase as they.see fit. Unbelievably priced and exceptional value. Lydia happened to be on break and suggested a few pieces that I nationally wouldn't order. After finishing the Trust Me, I had to force down as much as I could handle. She suggested the albacore belly. It was second to none. I'll out it up against Otoro or Chutoro any day. Can't get enough of this place. First stop and last stop on every trip to the city!  Don't walk by this place, you'll regret not going in sooner!!

We came in recently and were kinda anxious  about the wait time but it was so worth it. Lydia was our server and  she explained the menu very well and just made us feel at home. She recommended the albacore belly and it was so good. We definitely will come back.
Definitely a place be. Our server chey was great. First time eating sushi and she recommended kompachy and shutoro from the specials. they were equally amazing.

An Italian restaurant headed by actual Italians? Do you know how rare that is to find in NYC?

I'm so glad we spontaneously came here for dinner after an afternoon of frolicking through the Village. At ~5pm, we were seated pretty quickly (about 10-15 min after walking in)--had we delayed by even half an hour, we might as well have waited for hell to freeze over.

The Carciofi Fritti (fried artichoke hearts) were perfectly fried and tasty enough on their own, but when paired with the homemade garlic aioli sauce, they were everything you want fried vegetables to be.

Pasta-wise, the Amatriciana was all savory guanciale and al dente noodz with just the right dash of pecorino romano. The Pasticciata was creamier and meatier, and the Anolini Pasticciati was the meatiest one to rule them all.

I understand the social media hype circle recently made this place go viral because of its adorable ceiling-swing benches--and now every Gen Z and their cousin wants to film a TikTok of them eating pasta while swinging from fake greenery. That might explain why there was a nightclub-long line outside the restaurant by the time we left. *Cue the world's biggest eye roll*. I think we immediately endeared ourselves to our server by having no idea about any of this when he asked us directly--that might be why we were gifted with free limoncello at the end. The lesson is: Don't be sheeple. And eat lots of pasta.

What a hidden gem in NYC! Honestly, I wasn’t expecting to find such an authentic and unique place in such a touristy city, but Maestro Pasta completely surprised us!

Loved everything about the atmosphere, the beautiful decor, and especially the warm, welcoming feeling. The owner was there and spent some time chatting with us. Such a knowledgeable gentleman, genuinely passionate about his food and what they do. You can really feel that passion throughout the restaurant.

The food was absolutely delicious! The cured meats and prosciutto were amazing, and the fresh pasta, handmade right there, was just incredible. You can truly taste the difference. Simple, authentic Italian food done beautifully.

One little detail made the experience even more special. The staff brought a small piece of pasta dough for our three-year-old daughter to play with, and she absolutely loved it! She was entertained the entire time. Such a sweet, thoughtful gesture that made us feel right at home.

This is exactly the kind of restaurant I love discovering when travelling. Authentic food, passionate people, beautiful atmosphere, and genuine hospitality. A little piece of Italy in the middle of NYC. Can’t recommend it enough!

This place was way over priced for what it was. Pasta was good not great and cost around $30 for a small plate. As for service there was no check-in after food was served or offering a desert menu for our party. In this area there are much better Italian options around this price point.

Bright white cafe, dark (and harsh) coffee. MJ Cafe is a laptop warrior remote work cafe with a well designed and accommodating environment. Plants line the entrance, and it reads as “hip” (see the neon light cursive sign and Y2K music). Lounge area is homey and cute. Plant of seating is nice with classic bistro style tables. Drip coffee: Bitter, dark, a bit hard to drink. On paper, it’s a medium roast, but drinks like a dark roast. A bit nutty in taste. Unclear on where beans were from when I asked. Strange amount of bubbles on top of the coffee as well. Ownership can consider using a slightly lighter roast for a more balanced flavor; and extracting less from the beans (consider a few notches coarser in grind setting). People seemed to be having a nice experience hanging out there. Some nice amenities (water, bathroom). Drip coffee score: 3/5. Everything else score: 4.25/5. Overall score: 3.75/5.

This is the first time I've seen a Korean restaurant, where the average price is around $36, give a hard time to a customer just for asking for kimchi. It's a good thing it's in Manhattan, though. Tsk tsk. I've lived in New York for six years and have been to countless Korean restaurants from Midtown to Flushing, but this is seriously the first time I've encountered something like this.

I ordered the Pork Cutlet ($19) from the lunch menu and asked for kimchi, but the server called another staff member over. The new employee gave me a hard time, saying that kimchi is only included with the platter menu. It's not like this is my first time here; I had received kimchi with the pork cutlet on a previous visit, so I requested it. Even if the system has changed, I wonder if this is the right way to treat a customer. But isn't kimchi with pork cutlet the unwritten rule? I'm never going back.

BUYER BEWARE! This is NOT the original Tomoe Sushi.

I visited today and was so incredibly disappointed that I had to leave this review to warn others. The legendary OG Tomoe Sushi, which was run by the original Japanese owner, Ken-san with amazing quality for nearly 40 years, permanently closed in 2021.

This new place, "Tomo21 Sushi," is now run by new Chinese owners, Fei Chen and Guo Bin Chen. They deliberately chose a similar name and kept the old interior to trick people into thinking it's the same spot. The prices have gone way up, but the quality of the sushi has completely tanked compared to the past.
If you go in expecting the amazing food and memories from the original place, you will be deeply disappointed.

It might look like a great restaurant online because the reviews are mixed with the old Tomoe Sushi's legendary reviews, but do not be fooled. What they are doing right now is "review hijacking"—a clear violation of Google's policies.

I went to this restaurant today with a friend I hadn’t seen in months. We chose a table near the bar and spent the first few minutes catching up. After about 5 minutes, a server came over to ask if we were ready to order. We apologized and said we hadn’t looked at the menu yet, then started going through it.

Since we were in the mood for something seasonal, I thought I’d ask the server for recommendations. I tried getting his attention, but he didn’t seem particularly interested in acknowledging us. At one point he walked right past me and I said “Hey, I have a question.” Instead of responding he walked away to hand menus to another table. When he came back, he said, “And I have an answer.” His tone already felt a little off, but I brushed it off.

I asked if they had anything fall-themed on the menu, meaning seasonal dishes or ingredients. Pretty straightforward question. Instead of offering a recommendation or simply saying they didn’t have any seasonal specials, he responded with a condescending “What do you mean?” followed by a sarcastic “You want something with pumpkin?” I was genuinely caught off guard. I clarified that I meant seasonal ingredients, and instead of helping, he kept questioning me in a mocking tone saying “Oh yeah? I’d love to know which ingredients are seasonal.”

At that point, I was honestly speechless. English is my second language, and being put on the spot like that made it even harder to find my words. I really wasn’t expecting to be interrogated about seasonal produce and couldn’t even react. Eventually I started naming ingredients like root vegetables, asparagus, rosemary, thyme, walnuts, etc. He mentioned a couple of dishes, including a potato pizza with rosemary. When I asked where it was on their very crowded menu, he didn’t even bother pointing it out. He just repeated, “The potato pizza,” leaving me to find it myself.

The whole interaction felt unnecessarily rude, sarcastic, and condescending. My friend and I kept looking at each other in disbelief because neither of us could understand where this attitude was coming from. We had been perfectly polite and had barely interacted with him before this. We ended up deciding to leave without ordering.

Maybe next time I’ll just order a pumpkin pie pizza with lots of cinnamon on top. I’m sorry if you hate your job, and have a VERY happy fall season 🎃🍀

I've been sitting on this experience for almost two months and just can't shake it ... so I feel compelled to write this negative review. Just look at the incoherent reply to this review and you get all the information you need about this place. Pointing to the outside weather as the reason they are serving WARM drinks???? I, honestly, wouldn't feel comfortable drinking a beverage or eating food prepared by someone this incompetent. Good luck to anyone who goes here.

To set the scene, I had spent literally all day walking around Brooklyn in the sun and heat completing a scavenger hunt. I was hot and sweaty and just wanted to sit and have a chat with a friend over a refreshing, cold beverage. Literally all I could imagine en route to Black Crescent was a crisp, ice-cold Diet Coke. Of all the things I could have ordered, a Diet Coke is just about the simplest thing you can order at a bar. Not too much to ask for, right? Well, apparently it was. And for the record, my friend ordered alcoholic drinks and we ordered food ... didn't just come here for a soda. When I ordered my Diet Coke, what I got was something resembling brown water that tasted extremely watered down. So, I got up (didn't wave the bartender over) and politely told him the drink tasted really watered down. I can still see the look of annoyance he gave me clearly in my mind. I went back to my friend at our table. A few moments later, the bartender came out with a glass of ice and a glass of diet coke and plopped both on the table with an undeniably shitty attitude. Despite my treatment, I still remained polite, even though he was showing me less than no respect. With the components now separated for me to combine, it became clear what the problem was. The glass of Diet Coke wasn't just room temperature ... it was WARM. So, what had clearly happened was there were bottles of soft drinks being stored in the warm back room and being poured over ice and presented to customers as an appropriate drink. It isn't.

Not to spare words but how does that bartender still have a job? How lazy do you need to be to get annoyed at someone ordering a soft drink and then give them attitude when they are communicating a valid issue to you? I will never be coming back here. This bartender is mentioned in multiple negative reviews over the years but I guess the establishment just doesn't care. And one more thing. There's a special place in the afterlife for watering holes that serve soft drinks out of tiny cocktail glasses. Like, really? How is this place still in business?
